To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
100 ml of water or broth is adequate to recover salmonella from broiler carcasses when the organism is present at a level of 20 cells/carcass or higher.

sampling of broiler carcass for salmonella with 100 ml of water or enrichment medium will consistently detect salmonella inoculated at a rate of 20 cells/carcass, when the carcasses are stored at -23C for 3 to 6 months.
the smallest volume of rinse water that can consistently detect salmonella on inoculated broiler carcasses is 100 ml.

the development of an efficient and economical procedure for sampling broiler carcasses to determine the prevalence of salmonella on raw broiler carcasses.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
100 ml of rinsing medium is adequate for sampling of broiler carcass to recover Salmonella present on the carcass.
100 ml of rinse water is adequate to recover all Salmonella spp. that are present in numbers greater than 20 cells/carcass on broiler carcass surfaces.

100 ml of water is adequate to recover Salmonellae from freshly processed broilers, or carcasses that have been frozen for 3 or more months, when they are inoculated with as few as 20 cells per carcass.

a 100-ml rinse volume can be used in the detection of salmonella on broiler carcass surfaces.
a 100 ml volume of rinsing water or medium is adequate to detect Salmonella present on broiler chicken carcasses.

The main takeaway from our work is that
100 ml of rinsing fluid is sufficient to recover salmonella from broiler carcasses.

the volume of rinse water or medium used in carcass sampling procedures can be reduced to as low as 100 ml without sacrificing the ability of the procedure to recover salmonella from the raw broiler carcass.
